cevap: Sitting through that whole night while "everyone was drinking" and feeling "strange inside all night," even when nobody noticed, took real strength. That quiet effort still counts, even if no one else could see it.

It sounds like you're building real structure around your days, especially since you already know that "the empty hours are hard." Finding ways to get through those evening gaps is a caring thing to do for yourself.

It's understandable that you sometimes "forget" — keeping up with both appointments and daily routines is hard for anyone. A simple reminder set on your phone might take some of that pressure off your memory.
A house that's silent when you walk in and a silence that "weighs on" you like that sounds heavy to carry alone. Noticing how much it affects you shows how much you still care about your family.

Going from those three quiet months to actively "applying" now is already a big step forward. The silence from employers is discouraging, but it reflects the job market, not your effort or your worth.
Saying "part of that is my own fault" takes real honesty, and that same honesty could be the first step toward reconnecting. One call from you might be all it takes to start things moving again.

Those two days when you "couldn't tell anyone why" sound like they were incredibly heavy to get through on your own. You don't need to explain everything right away — it's okay to talk about it whenever you feel ready.

Carrying something this big alone, especially with the fear that "if I say it and fail it will be worse," sounds exhausting. Telling someone doesn't have to mean risking failure — it could also mean finally getting support you don't have right now.

It's great that you've found something that works, walking in the morning and taking "a short round" in the evening so your mind settles at night. That's a healthy way to take care of both your body and your thoughts.
It makes sense to feel like you're "giving an account of myself," even when you know they "mean well." It might help to gently tell them what kind of support actually feels good to you right now.

Quitting both smoking and coffee at once took a lot of determination, and it's completely normal to feel unsure "what to do in the mornings" while things settle. Give yourself time to find a new rhythm — it will come.

Nights spent staring "at the ceiling" and mornings when you feel like you "never rested" sound utterly draining. Please be gentle with yourself through this — your body and mind are clearly asking for some extra care.
